title: Tajwid, a first taste
hook: recitation has rules of sound: stretching, nasal hums, stops
carry: every letter is due its right

segments.voice: Yesterday, the three quls: say, say, say, three times at morning and evening. Your line was three times, three. How long did it really take last night? Day two hundred twenty-eight.

Put on a recording of the Qur'an recited well, and listen for a minute without trying to understand a word. It isn't quite singing, and it isn't quite speaking. Some vowels stretch, long and steady, like a held note. Some sounds hum in the nose for a beat. Then the voice stops, exactly, and breathes, and starts again. It sounds free, but it isn't improvised. Every one of those stretches and hums follows a rule, and tradition says the rules have been handed down teacher to student, by ear, the way a child in a mosque class still learns them. Today: tajwid, a first taste.
screen: `NOT SINGING, NOT SPEAKING.` → `STRETCHES, HUMS AND STOPS.` → `RULES HANDED DOWN.`

segments.voice: Tajwid comes from the root j-w-d, to make good, to make excellent. Jayyid, good, is from the same root. So tajwid is making the recitation good: giving the words the sound they were given in. Tajwid manuals, tradition says, define it with a line that became our carry: giving every letter its right and its due. Its right is how it's made: where in the throat, the tongue, the lips or the nose each letter lives. Its due is what happens to it next to other letters. Three rules make a first taste. One, madd, stretching. A long vowel is held for two beats, and in some places four or six. Listen to the end of the Fatiha, wa lad-daaaallin: that long a is held for six. Two, ghunnah, the nasal hum. When a noon or a meem is doubled, as in inna, the sound rests in the nose for two beats. Three, waqf, stopping. Small marks above the line tell the reciter where a stop is required, where it's allowed, and where stopping would bend the meaning. The Qur'an itself asks for this care: in Surah al-Muzzammil, recite the Qur'an with tartil, measured and distinct. Scholars say avoiding mistakes that change meaning is required; the finer rules are a craft, learned by ear from a teacher, often with a chain of teachers going back generations. And here is the kindest hadith for beginners. Bukhari and Muslim record the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ saying that the one skilled in the Qur'an is with the noble, righteous scribes, and the one who stumbles through it, finding it hard, gets two rewards.
screen: `J-W-D — TO MAKE EXCELLENT.` · `MADD — THE STRETCH.` · `GHUNNAH — THE HUM.` · `WAQF — THE STOP.` · then, large: `EVERY LETTER IS DUE ITS RIGHT.`

segments.voice: Sit, and just listen inwardly. Say the word Allah slowly in your mind, or aloud if you're alone, and notice the long a in the middle. Let it stretch, two beats, like a breath held gently. Then hum, mmm, with your lips closed, and feel where it sits: in the nose, behind the face. That's the place ghunnah lives. Then stop, completely, and let the silence be exact. Stretch, hum, stop. Do it a few times, slowly, as if every sound had a right to be heard in full. The bell holds the time.
Tajwid. Making excellent: the rules of Qur'an recitation, the stretch, the hum and the stop, so every letter gets its right. Today's word.

Your line: every letter is due its right. Today, listen to one short recitation, and catch one stretched vowel, the held note. Then, in one conversation, give someone's words their full length before you answer. Day two hundred twenty-eight.

howItsDone: Muslims learn tajwid from a teacher, usually by ear and repetition, often in mosque classes or with a local reciter; advanced students may receive an ijazah, a license to teach recitation, with a chain of teachers going back many generations.

original.note: Arabic: making excellent, from j-w-d; the rules of Qur'an recitation.

trapdoor: what you thought: a style of chanting the Qur'an.
what it means: rules for every sound, the stretch, the hum and the stop, giving each letter its right.
what a scholar hears: haqq and mustahaqq, the letter's own features and those it takes from neighbors; tartil in 73:4; transmission by ijazah.
